name: Pagan / Handfasting
blurb: A circle cast outdoors, hands bound with cord, and a legal position that depends entirely on which side of the border you stand.

events.name: Meeting the celebrant
events.description: Pagan ceremonies are written rather than inherited. Expect several long conversations building the rite from your two paths, which may not be the same tradition as each other.

events.name: The legal marriage
events.when: Before, or as part of, the day
events.description: In Scotland a registered Pagan celebrant can solemnise a legal marriage anywhere. In England and Wales they cannot, so the legal marriage is a separate register office appointment.

events.name: The handfasting
events.description: A circle is cast, the quarters called, vows exchanged and the couple's hands bound with cords. Often ends with jumping the broom. Traditionally held outdoors, and traditionally at a point in the wheel of the year that means something.

events.name: The feast
events.description: Usually informal, often outdoors, frequently involving mead.

events.name: A stated term
events.description: Some handfastings are made for a year and a day, or another agreed term, renewed thereafter. Others are for life. This is a decision to make explicitly, and to explain to relatives who will otherwise misunderstand it.

items.name: Celebrant's fee
items.note: Pagan celebrants write the rite with you over months rather than delivering a template, and price accordingly.

items.name: Register office ceremony and certificates
items.note: In England and Wales the legal marriage is separate. In Scotland, if your celebrant is registered, this line disappears.

items.name: Outdoor site hire or permission
items.note: Woodland, stone circle, beach or hilltop. Many sites need written permission, and popular ancient sites have their own booking systems and restrictions.

items.name: Handfasting cords
items.note: Often hand-braided by the couple or given by family, in colours chosen for their meanings. Kept afterwards.

items.name: Altar, quarter candles and tools
items.note: Candles or lanterns for the four quarters, a chalice, a besom. Outdoors, everything must survive wind.

items.name: The besom
items.note: For jumping the broom at the close. Often made or gifted rather than bought.

items.name: Weather cover
items.note: A yurt, tipi or marquee. Outdoor ceremonies in Britain need a plan that is not 'hope'.

items.name: Generators and lighting
items.note: A field has no power. Music, catering and lighting all need it.

items.name: Toilet hire
items.note: Non-negotiable at an outdoor site, and your guests will thank you.

items.name: Catering
items.note: Often relaxed — hog roast, sharing tables, foraged and seasonal touches. Cater properly for vegans; many Pagan guests are.

items.name: Mead, cider and drinks
items.note: Mead in the chalice for the ceremony, and usually rather more of it afterwards.

items.name: Cake
items.note: Often made by family, and frequently seasonal rather than iced.

items.name: Wedding outfit
items.note: Anything from a medieval-styled gown to a suit and bare feet. Practical footwear for uneven ground matters more than at most weddings.

items.name: Second outfit
items.note: A change for the feast, or simply warmer layers once the sun goes.

items.name: Flowers and greenery
items.note: Seasonal and often foraged. Flower crowns are near-universal.

items.name: Rings
items.note: Exchanged at the legal ceremony, at the handfasting, or both.

items.name: Photographer
items.note: Find one comfortable outdoors in poor weather who understands not to walk through a cast circle.

items.name: Videographer
items.note: Worth it outdoors, where the wind takes half the spoken vows away from anyone standing at the back.

items.name: Musicians
items.note: Live folk, drumming and a fire are the usual shape of the evening.

items.name: Fire pit and wood
items.note: Central to most handfastings, and the thing most sites have rules about. Get permission in writing.

items.name: Invitations
items.note: Explain the format. Many guests will never have attended a handfasting and will want to know what to wear and whether to stand.

items.name: Transport and parking
items.note: Remote sites mean parking on grass, shuttle runs and a plan for when it rains.

items.name: Event insurance and site permissions
items.note: Landowner permission in writing, public liability cover, and any licence needed for alcohol or amplified music.

items.name: Hair and make-up
items.note: Choose products that survive wind and rain. Outdoor ceremonies are unforgiving.

items.name: Contingency
items.note: Outdoors in Britain. Hold a real reserve, not a token one.

timeline.task: Establish the legal position first: in Scotland a registered Pagan celebrant can marry you anywhere; in England and Wales they cannot and you need a separate register office ceremony
Find a celebrant whose tradition sits comfortably with both of yours, and meet them before booking anything
Choose the site and get the landowner's permission in writing — walk it for vehicle access, ground conditions and a wet-weather position
If you want a date on the wheel of the year, remember Beltane and the solstices are the busiest days in the Pagan calendar
Decide whether the handfasting is for life or for a stated term, and agree how you will explain it to family
Book the shelter — a yurt, tipi or marquee is a plan; an optimistic forecast is not
Book generators, toilets and lighting for a site that has none of them
Arrange event insurance and any licence for alcohol or amplified music
Confirm fire permissions in writing, including what may be burned and how late
Book the caterer and confirm proper vegan provision rather than one dish
Make or commission the cords, and choose the colours together
Book a photographer who works outdoors in bad light and knows not to cross a cast circle
Book the register office appointment for the legal marriage, if you are in England or Wales
Send invitations explaining the format, the ground underfoot and what to wear
Write the rite with your celebrant — vows, quarter calls, who speaks and when
Plan the wet-weather version of every part of the day, and tell suppliers what it is
Confirm parking, shuttles and where cars go if the field is soft
Walk the site again with the celebrant and mark the circle
Confirm final numbers and the mead
Register the legal marriage and collect the certificate

paperwork.note: A Pagan handfasting has no legal effect in England and Wales. The legal marriage is a separate register office ceremony, and you must give at least 29 clear days' notice.

Scotland recognises belief-based marriages, and celebrants of some Pagan bodies are registered to solemnise legal marriages anywhere. Confirm your individual celebrant's registration, not just their organisation's.
For any outdoor site. Verbal permission from a farmer is not a booking, and does not survive the farm changing hands.
Usually required by the landowner, and sensible regardless on uneven ground with open fire.

paperwork.item: Licence for alcohol or amplified music
paperwork.note: A temporary event notice, where you are selling alcohol or amplifying music at an unlicensed site.
Written, specific, and including what may be burned and until when.

paperwork.item: Evidence of the ending of any previous marriage

paperwork.note: Collect the certified copy. A handfasting alone leaves you legally unmarried in England and Wales.

customs.name: Casting the circle
customs.description: The ceremony space is marked and consecrated, and the four quarters — earth, air, fire, water — are called. Guests are usually asked not to cross the boundary once it is cast.

customs.name: The cords
customs.description: Hands are bound with cords, often several, each colour chosen for a meaning and sometimes tied by a different family member. This is where 'tying the knot' comes from.

customs.name: Jumping the broom
customs.description: The couple leap the besom together to close the rite and cross into married life. Also found in African-American wedding tradition, from a separate history.

customs.name: A year and a day
customs.description: Some handfastings are made for a stated term and renewed. Others are for life. Neither is more authentic, but the difference badly confuses relatives if it is not explained.

customs.name: The wheel of the year
customs.description: Beltane at the start of May is the traditional handfasting season, and the solstices are popular. These are the busiest dates for celebrants and sites.

customs.name: Oathing stone
customs.description: Vows are said with a hand on a stone, which is then kept.

customs.name: The chalice
customs.description: Mead or wine shared from a single cup, sometimes with a libation poured to the land first.

customs.name: Barefoot
customs.description: Many couples handfast barefoot to be in contact with the ground. Worth checking what the ground actually is first.

gotchas: In England and Wales a handfasting is not a legal marriage, whoever conducts it. You need a register office ceremony as well, and many couples do it quietly a day or two before.

Scotland is different: registered celebrants of some Pagan bodies can solemnise a legal marriage anywhere, indoors or out. Confirm your individual celebrant's registration rather than assuming their organisation covers them.
An outdoor site is a build, not a venue. Power, water, toilets, parking, shelter and a wet-weather plan are all yours to arrange and all cost real money.
Landowner permission must be in writing. Verbal agreement does not survive a change of mind, a change of ownership or a wet spring.
Beltane and the solstices are the busiest dates in the calendar. Celebrants and popular sites book a year or more ahead for them.
Ancient monuments and stone circles have custodians, booking systems and restrictions, and most do not permit what people imagine they do.
Fire is central and is the thing sites regulate hardest. Get written permission covering what may be burned and how late.
A stated-term handfasting will be misread by relatives as a trial marriage unless you explain it plainly in advance.
Cater seriously for vegans rather than adding one dish. A significant proportion of guests at a Pagan wedding will be.
Guests will not know the etiquette — whether to enter the circle, when to stand, whether to speak. A short note with the invitation solves it.

Wiccan.label: Wiccan

addCustoms.name: Great Rite in token
addCustoms.description: The chalice and blade, performed symbolically, closing the rite.

addGotchas: Wiccan practice varies between traditions and covens. Ask your celebrant which form they work in.

Druid.label: Druid

addCustoms.name: The Gorsedd prayer and the circle of stones
addCustoms.description: Druid rites frequently open with a peace prayer to the four directions and use a stone circle, real or laid for the day.

addGotchas: The Druid Network is a registered religious charity in England and Wales, but that does not make a Druid celebrant able to solemnise a legal marriage there. It still needs a separate civil ceremony.

Heathen.label: Heathen

addCustoms.name: The oath ring and the sumbel
addCustoms.description: Oaths sworn on a ring, and a formal round of toasts to gods, ancestors and the couple.

addGotchas: Heathen practice is oath-centred, and a sumbel with real toasts and real drink needs planning into the running order rather than bolting on.
